title: How Esther Ocloo Turned Ten Shillings Into Twelve Jars of Marmalade
dek: During the Second World War a scholarship girl in Accra turned an aunt's gift into twelve jars of marmalade, then a school contract and a military one.

story.event: Selling marmalade made with an aunt's ten shillings, then winning school and military juice contracts
story.summary: In the early 1940s Esther Nkulenu (later Ocloo), a Cadbury scholarship girl recently out of Achimota School, spent part of ten shillings from an aunt on oranges, sugar and twelve jars, and sold marmalade in Accra despite classmates' ridicule. Her old school gave her a contract to supply it, then helped her into orange juice and a contract to supply troops during the Second World War, which she met with a temporary factory and goods bought on credit; the business became Nkulenu Industries. She later became the first chair of Women's World Banking.
paragraphs: In the early 1940s a young woman not long out of Achimota School walked near the government offices in Accra with twelve jars of orange marmalade at a shilling each. Esther Nkulenu, later Esther Ocloo, was the daughter of poor farmers from Peki in the Volta region. A Cadbury scholarship had paid for her schooling, and her mother had seen her off to Accra with a sixpence. Living with relatives, she had been given ten shillings by an aunt. She spent six of them on sugar, firewood, oranges and jars, she later recalled, determined to "turn that 10 shillings into two pounds at least."

She knew what an educated girl was expected to do, and it was not this. "I was ridiculed by all my classmates, who saw me hawking marmalade on the street like an uneducated street vendor," she said. She had learned the recipe in home science lessons; she kept going and put the profits back into the business. Then her old school asked her to bring a sample to the dining hall and offered her a contract to supply it. That, she said in 1990, "put some confidence in me."

The school pressed juice from its own orange trees and suggested she do the same. Its staff showed her how, and passed on a letter from military officers who wanted a regular supply of orange juice for troops stationed in the colony during the Second World War. She spent her savings on a temporary factory to qualify for the contract, then found she could not afford the materials. In her own account, she showed the contract to a store manager and bought on credit. Soon she held her first cheque, "I'd never seen one before," and her aunt and uncle opened a bank account for her. The business carried her family name: Nkulenu.

Credit stayed hard. When she later wanted a bank loan to mechanise, she had nothing to pledge: her father's house, she said, would not sell for $50, and she was not married. Officials eventually intervened. After six years in business she went to Britain to study food preservation, and in 1979 she became the first chair of Women's World Banking, an idea her own struggle for a loan had helped to shape.

quote.text: Here shall no end be hindered, no hope marred, No loss be feared: faith--yea, a little faith-- Shall save thee from the anguish of thy dread.
quote.source_title: The Song Celestial; Or, Bhagavad-Gîtâ, tr. Sir Edwin Arnold, Project Gutenberg eBook #2388
quote.connection: Krishna tells Arjuna that on this path no effort is lost and even a little carries a person past fear. Ocloo began with very little: ten shillings, twelve jars and, later, a temporary factory. What the first school contract gave her, by her own account, was confidence.

reflection: Ocloo's classmates saw a girl with a good education selling jam on the street and drew the obvious conclusion. She drew a different one, and the first people to agree with her were the ones who tasted the marmalade, not the ones who judged the job.

Some of what you are building may look, to people who knew you in training or at work, like a step sideways from a respectable path. Their view is real, and it can sting. It is also not the test. The test is whether what you make is good enough that someone asks for more of it.
invitation: Think of one small thing you have made recently that you have been shy to show. Give it, or a sample of it, to one person today who would actually use it, and ask what they would change.

cross_checks.claim: Ocloo started with ten shillings from an aunt and made twelve jars of marmalade, sold at a shilling each.
Her former school gave her a contract to supply marmalade and then orange juice.
She then won a contract to supply orange juice to the military during the Second World War.
Her school was Achimota, which she attended on a Cadbury scholarship.
Classmates ridiculed her for selling marmalade instead of taking an office job.
Ocloo was the first chair of Women's World Banking, founded in 1979.

research_notes: Starting sum: Ocloo's 1990 account to the Christian Science Monitor, the 2002 New York Times obituary, Citi Newsroom and Mental Floss all give ten shillings from an aunt; Mental Floss quotes a later interview in which she says she spent six shillings on ingredients; Women's World Banking's 2024 page opens with 'a mere sixpence', which appears to conflate the aunt's gift with the sixpence her mother gave her for school (both CSM and the NYT mention the sixpence separately); Al Jazeera says only 'a few' shillings. The story uses ten shillings, six of them spent. Financing the military contract: in her own 1990 account she showed the contract to a store manager and bought materials on credit, and later struggled to get a bank loan for lack of collateral until officials intervened so she could mechanise; the NYT obituary, Al Jazeera, Mental Floss and Citi Newsroom say a bank lent on the strength of the contract(s). The story follows her own account and does not say a bank financed the first contract. Military customer: CSM says 'West Africa Volunteer Forces'; Wikipedia, citing the Dictionary of African Biography, says the Royal West African Frontier Force; the story says only 'military officers' and 'troops stationed in the colony'. Year: Al Jazeera says the Nkulenu business was established in 1942; Wikipedia says she began selling marmalade in 1943; CSM says 'during World War II'. The story says 'the early 1940s' and approx_date is 1942. School: CSM and the NYT do not name it; Citi Newsroom (Cadbury scholarship to Achimota in 1936), Mental Floss and Wikipedia name Achimota. Age at death differs (82 in most sources, 83 in the NYT headline); not used. Women's World Banking's founding: the NYT says founded in 1979 with Ocloo as chair; CSM says she was first chair 1979-85; Wikipedia says co-founded 1976; the story says she became first chair in 1979. The link between her loan difficulties and Women's World Banking is from CSM ('played a role in the decision'). The NYT obituary is cited from a Ghanaian newspaper's reproduction because nytimes.com blocks automated requests. 'Funding: bootstrapped' reflects the aunt's gift, savings and supplier credit. The Gita verse comes from Krishna's teaching on the yoga of action and is applied here by analogy.
